candidate_sources.title: Birch - Marssonina Leaf Spot - Cooperative Extension: Insect Pests, Ticks and Plant Diseases - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Small dark-brown spots, often with yellow margins, develop on young leaves in spring; spots may coalesce to form larger lesions. The fungus Marssonina betulae overwinters in infected leaf debris and shoots; spores are dispersed by wind and rain, infecting new leaves under wet conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Identify and Manage Marssonina Leaf Spot on trees and shrubs - Purdue Plant Doctor
candidate_sources.snippet: Initial symptoms are small black spots that enlarge and join together as a mass of necrotic tissue, with complete defoliation occurring during summer. Marssonina overwinters in cankers on small stems; spores are produced in spring and summer. Pruning out cankered stems and destroying infected leaf litter are the most effective controls.

candidate_sources.snippet: Marssonina leaf spot is a fungal disease that produces small dark spots on leaves which may coalesce, leading to premature leaf drop. Management includes raking and destroying fallen leaves and maintaining tree vigor.

candidate_sources.title: Birch Leaf Spot Disease - Elmsavers
candidate_sources.snippet: Birch Leaf Spot (Marssonina betulae). Small dark-brown spots with yellow margins develop on young leaves; spots coalesce and cause complete defoliation in summer. Mainly affects European birch species such as Betula pendula 'Silver', 'Dalecarlica', and Young's Weeping Birch 'Youngii'.

candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Phyllactinia guttata covering Identity, Overview, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected (including Betulaceae: Betula, Carpinus, Corylus, Ostrya), Diagnosis, and Further Information. Causes powdery mildew on a broad range of hardwood trees including birch.

candidate_sources.title: Phyllactinia guttata - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Phyllactinia guttata is a species of powdery mildew fungus in the family Erysiphaceae. It causes powdery mildew on leaves and stems of a broad range of hosts including the Betulaceae (Betula, Carpinus, Corylus, Ostrya). White powdery growth occurs on either leaf surface and on catkins; dark spherical chasmothecia form on the underside of leaves late in the growing season; conidia are wind disseminated.

candidate_sources.title: Identification of Powdery Mildew Fungi
candidate_sources.snippet: APS Education Center resource on identifying powdery mildew fungi. White to gray powdery patches appear on affected plant tissues; on trees and shrubs Phyllactinia is among the most common powdery mildew fungi with birch a common host. White powdery appearance is due to conidia borne in chains; wind-borne spores do not require free water for germination; new conidia produced every 3 to 14 days.
